title: Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended II
description: Brute force to optimized: unmemoized recursion with a linear scan versus a memoized DP over (index, remaining picks) with binary search for the next valid event.

content.title: Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended II

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given events where events[i] = [startDay, endDay, value], and an integer k, you may attend at most k events. You cannot attend two events with overlapping days (unless one ends exactly when the other starts, which is still considered non-overlapping here). Return the MAXIMUM total value achievable.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Select non-overlapping intervals maximizing value, limited to k selections\"","A DP over (event index, remaining picks), similar to House Robber but with a \"jump to next non-conflicting\" step"],["\"Find the next event starting after this one ends\"","Binary search on sorted start times finds this jump target in O(log n)"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

This combines two classic ideas: choosing a subset of non-overlapping intervals (like Non-overlapping Intervals), and limiting the choice to at most k selections (like a knapsack-style constraint). Sorting events by start day, then deciding for each whether to skip it or take it (jumping to the next valid event via binary search), with a remaining-picks counter, captures both constraints.

blocks.title: Analogy: Choosing the Best k Non-Overlapping Job Offers
blocks.text: Picture being offered many jobs, each spanning specific days and paying a certain amount, wanting to choose at most k of them (since you only have that much attention to give) without any day overlaps, maximizing total pay. Considering jobs in start-day order, and for each deciding to skip it or take it (using up one of your k slots and jumping past its conflicting days), captures the full decision space.

blocks.caption: For each event in start-day order, decide to skip it or take it (using a pick, jumping to the next valid event)

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Result: 7. Attending event [1,2,4] and event [3,4,3] (non-overlapping, since one ends at 2 and the next starts at 3) gives 4+3=7.
5. How Should We Think?

Before trying every subset of up to k events, notice this decomposes into a DP over (current event index, remaining picks): for each event, either skip it (move to the next event, same picks remaining) or take it (add its value, use up one pick, and jump to the first event starting after this one ends, found via binary search).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Sorting events by start day lets the events be processed in a fixed left-to-right order, a prerequisite for a clean DP formulation.

Observation 2: For the current event (at index i, with picks remaining k), there are exactly two choices: skip it (recurse on i+1, k unchanged), or take it (add its value, recurse on the index of the first event starting after this one ends, with k-1 picks remaining).

Observation 3: The best value at (i, k) is the maximum of these two choices; the base case is running out of events or picks, contributing 0.

Observation 4: Finding "the first event starting after this one ends" is exactly a binary search on the sorted start times, since events are sorted by start day; memoizing on (i, k) avoids recomputing overlapping subproblems.

This leads to sorting events by start day, then a memoized DP over (event index, remaining picks): skip or take (using binary search to jump to the next valid event when taking), maximizing total value.
6. Brute Force Solution
Recursively try every subset of up to k non-overlapping events directly, without memoization or binary search, tracking the maximum total value.
Step by step algorithm

items: For each event, recursively try skipping it, or taking it and scanning forward for the next non-overlapping event (using a linear scan, not binary search).
Track the maximum achievable total value across all valid combinations, capped at k picks.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Directly implementing the skip/take recursion correctly explores every possible valid combination.

Without memoization, the same (index, remaining) subproblems are recomputed repeatedly, and without binary search, finding the next valid event costs O(n) each time, together giving exponential-ish blowup.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential without memoization (each event branches into 2 choices, n levels deep).
Space: O(n) recursion depth.

Limitation: memoizing on (index, remaining picks) avoids recomputation, and binary searching for the next valid event (since events are sorted) replaces the O(n) linear scan with O(log n), together achieving O(n times k times log n).
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why unmemoized recursion is wasteful: the same (event index, remaining picks) state can be reached via multiple different skip/take sequences, and recomputing it every time wastes enormous effort.

Adding memoization: caching the result of dp(i, remaining) the first time it is computed means each distinct state is only ever computed once, bounding the total states to O(n times k).

Speeding up the "next valid event" lookup: since events are sorted by start day, binary searching for the first index with a start day strictly greater than the current event's end day replaces an O(n) linear scan with O(log n).

The core idea: sort once, memoize the DP over (index, remaining picks), and binary search for the jump target when taking an event.

Sort events by start day. Define dp(i, remaining) as the best value using events from index i onward, with "remaining" picks left: max of skipping (dp(i+1, remaining)) or taking (event value plus dp(binary-searched next index, remaining-1)). Memoize by (i, remaining).

blocks.caption: Memoized DP over (index, remaining picks), using binary search to jump to the next non-overlapping event

blocks.text: Why This Works

Sorting events by start day makes the "skip or take, jump to the next valid event" decision well-defined and monotonic in index. Memoizing on (index, remaining picks) ensures each distinct subproblem is solved exactly once, since the same state can otherwise be reached via many different sequences of skip/take decisions. Binary searching for the next non-overlapping event exploits the sorted start times to replace an O(n) scan with O(log n), and combined with memoization, bounds the total work to O(n times k times log n).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k times log n), for the memoized states each requiring a binary search.
Space: O(n times k) for the memoization table.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended II combines three techniques into one solution: sorting to enable ordered processing, dynamic programming with memoization over (index, remaining picks) to avoid recomputation, and binary search to quickly find the next non-conflicting event.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to sort events by start day first, which the entire skip/take/binary-search structure depends on.
Using a strict binary search comparison inconsistent with the problem's definition of "non-overlapping" (events touching at a single day boundary should be considered non-overlapping here).

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["k equals events.length with no overlaps at all","All events can be attended, and the sum of all values is returned."],["k = 1","Reduces to simply picking the single highest-value event."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly naming the three combined techniques (sort, memoized DP over index and remaining picks, binary search for the jump) demonstrates a clear, structured understanding of why this harder problem needs more machinery than simpler interval problems.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "select at most k non-overlapping intervals maximizing value", think: sort by start, memoized DP over (index, remaining picks), binary search for the next valid event when taking one.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you adapt this to also report WHICH events were chosen, not just the total value?
How would you solve the k=1 special case (Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended, a related but distinct problem) differently?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Non-overlapping Intervals and House Robber, both contributing structural pieces (interval selection, bounded picks) to this combined problem.
Any "select up to k non-overlapping items maximizing value" problem, solvable via this same sort-DP-binary-search combination.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Unmemoized recursion with linear scanning costs exponential time; the memoized DP with binary search costs O(n times k times log n) time and O(n times k) space, the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: sort by start day, memoized DP over (event index, remaining picks), binary search to jump to the next non-overlapping event.
Core Idea: for each event, take the max of skipping it or taking it (adding its value and jumping past conflicting events, using up one pick).
Time: exponential for the unmemoized brute force, O(n times k times log n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) recursion depth versus O(n times k) for the memo table.
Most Important Observation: combining sorting, memoized DP, and binary search is necessary since each technique alone addresses only part of the problem's combined constraints.
Interview Difficulty: a genuinely hard problem, testing the ability to combine multiple techniques into one cohesive solution.
One line memory trick: sort, memoize dp(index, picks left), binary search the jump when taking an event.
